articles.title: UPSC Editorial Analysis: EOS-05 Mission and India's Geostationary Earth Observation Capabilities
articles.content: General Studies-3; Topic: Science and Technology- developments and their applications and effects in everyday life. Introduction The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has placed EOS-05 (Earth Observation Satellite-05) into its designated geostationary orbit (~36,000 km above Earth) following its launch aboard GSLV-F17 and the completion of its final orbit-raising maneuvers. As the second operational craft in the GISAT (Geo-Imaging Satellite) series, EOS-05 is India’s first operational imaging satellite positioned in a high-altitude geostationary orbit. About EOS-05 Mission and India’s Geostationary Earth Observation Capabilities EOS-05 , India’s first geostationary imaging satellite at ~36,000 km, provides continuous, real-time monitoring over the subcontinent. This fundamentally upgrades disaster management, agriculture, and strategic border surveillance beyond low-Earth-orbit limitations. Understanding EOS-05: Technological Framework Orbital Profile: Orbiting at ~36,000 km in synchronization with Earth’s rotation (geosynchronous/geostationary regime), the satellite maintains a permanent, fixed footprint over the Indian subcontinent and surrounding oceanic regions. Mass & Launch Platform: Weighing 2,367 kg, it was lofted using the Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) equipped with an indigenous cryogenic upper stage (C39/CE-7.5 class). Payload Instrumentation: Multi-spectral Visible and Near-Infrared (VNIR): High temporal resolution for surface tracking. Short-Wave Infrared (SWIR) & Thermal Infrared (TIR): Day-and-night thermal profiling, cloud microphysics, and surface heat emissions. Hyperspectral Sensors: Fine spectral signatures across contiguous narrow bands to distinguish crop types, soil mineral compositions, and water pollutant levels. Strategic & Multi-Dimensional Significance Disaster Risk Reduction (Sendai Framework Coherence) Cyclone Tracking: Continuous observation captures rapid cyclogenesis, cloud wall evolution, and landfall vectoring in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea without gaps between orbital passes. Flood & Inundation Mapping: Near real-time imaging of swelling river basins (e.g., Brahmaputra, Mahanadi) supports the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) with rapid evacuation corridors. Forest Fire Containment: Thermal bands detect sudden surface heat spikes, alerting forest departments before local canopies burn out of control. Strategic Surveillance & National Security Border Perimeter Awareness: Persistent gaze covers high-altitude friction points across the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and Line of Control (LoC). Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA): Continuous optical and infrared coverage monitors sea lines of communication (SLOCs), choke points (e.g., Malacca Strait approach), and unauthorized vessel movement across the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Agriculture & Economic Resilience Crop Stress Analysis: Hyperspectral imaging differentiates water stress, pest infestation, and nitrogen deficits across cropping belts. Yield Modeling: Real-time data streamlines the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) by replacing manual crop-cutting experiments with objective satellite indices for damage claims. Water Resource Accounting: Continuous monitoring tracks reservoir replenishment, glacier retreat in the Himalayas, and seasonal lake shrinkages. Weather Forecasting & Climate Change Studies High-cadence atmospheric imagery feeds directly into Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) models at the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting ( NCMRWF), refining monsoon onset forecasts and cloudburst warnings. Institutional & Strategic Redemption for ISRO The operationalization of EOS-05 restores operational momentum following two launcher setbacks: The PSLV-C61 (EOS-09) & PSLV-C62 (EOS-N1) Anomalies: Failures traceable to the third stage (PS3 solid motor) challenged the reliability narrative of ISRO’s workhorse launcher,...

articles.title: Engineers Day 2026: Who Was A. Lalitha? Meet India's First Female Engineer - Jagran Josh
articles.content: Engineers Day 2026: As India celebrates National Engineer’s Day on September 15, the spotlight is not only on the country’s celebrated engineers but also on the pioneers who broke barriers to enter a profession dominated by men. One such name is Ayyalasomayajula Lalitha, remembered as India’s first female engineer. Born in 1919 in Madras, now Chennai, Lalitha entered the field of electrical engineering at a time when engineering education and professional careers were largely considered a male domain. Her journey was particularly remarkable because she pursued engineering after becoming a young widow and mother. Her determination eventually took her to the College of Engineering, Guindy, where she graduated in electrical engineering in 1943. Exclusive: NBEMS NEET PG Answer Key 2026 at natboard.edu.in LIVE Who Was A. Lalitha? Ayyalasomayajula Lalitha was an Indian electrical engineer who became a pioneer for women in engineering. Born on August 27, 1919, in Madras, she belonged to a Telugu-speaking family. Her father, Pappu Subba Rao, was an engineering professor and encouraged her to continue her education. Lalitha was married at the age of 15 and became a mother soon after. Her husband died when she was still very young, leaving her to raise her daughter. Instead of giving up her education, she chose to continue studying and eventually pursued engineering. Her decision was significant for the period because professional engineering was overwhelmingly male-dominated. Lalitha went on to study at the College of Engineering, Guindy (CEG) in Chennai, becoming the first woman to graduate from the institution as an engineer. A. Lalitha Became India’s First Female Engineer in 1943 Lalitha graduated with a degree in Electrical Engineering in 1943, earning her place in Indian engineering history as the country's first female engineer. Her achievement came at a time when very few women had access to professional technical education. She studied in an institution where the overwhelming majority of students were men. The college administration also made arrangements for her accommodation during her studies. Lalitha's achievement was followed by the entry of other women into engineering. P.K. Thressia and Leelamma George Koshie were among the early women engineers associated with CEG, marking an important moment in the history of women in Indian engineering. Exclusive: CAT Exam 2026 Registration Last Date LIVE From Engineering College to Railway Workshop After completing her engineering education, Lalitha underwent practical training at the Jamalpur Railway Workshop, gaining hands-on experience in engineering. She later worked with the Central Standards Organisation in Shimla and also contributed to technical research with her father. Her early career demonstrated that her engineering degree was not merely a historic achievement. Lalitha went on to work in technical roles and build a professional career in a field where women were still rare. A. Lalitha’s Role in Bhakra Nangal Dam Project One of the most notable phases of Lalitha's professional career came after she joined Associated Electrical Industries (AEI) in Calcutta in 1948. articles.title: Isro's challenge: Indian space station as ISS successor
articles.content: Last week in Bengaluru, Sunita Williams flagged the “rigidity and bureaucracy” on the International Space Station, the habitable spacecraft circling Earth aboard which she has spent a total of 608 days. The former Nasa astronaut expressed hope that the inhabitants of future space stations would enjoy more freedom to analyse and decide, rather than having to depend on ground control stations. She highlighted the lack of access to previous ISS experiments’ database, which needs to be sourced from terrestrial centres, making continuity in space-based experiments difficult. The ISS, which has hosted humans since 2000, is currently planned to remain operational till 2030 end, extendable to 2032. Williams’ observation, made at the 9 th Bengaluru Space Expo, put the limelight on future space stations, including India’s 52-tonne, ₹20,000-crore Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), which the Indian Space Research Organisation plans to operationalise by 2035. The discussion must goad Isro into systematically preparing to make BAS the ideal successor to the ISS, as many international astronauts have already expressed willingness to work on the Indian station. Isro is not alone in the fray. Vast Space, an American company, plans to launch its first commercial space station, Haven 1, in 2027 as a precursor to larger modular artificial-gravity habitats. Although Isro has nine years before the scheduled BAS launch, much needs to be done in the intervening period. Gaganyaan, India’s first manned space mission, is scheduled in early 2027. Isro has already demonstrated autonomous orbital docking and undocking capability in January-April 2025, but has not yet tried it in a live mission using operational-scale capsules. This application will be crucial while assembling the BAS in space, and in ferrying astronauts and equipment to and from it. This technology will also be vital for the Chandrayaan-4 lunar soil sample mission in 2027-28. The first of BAS’s five modules, weighing 10 tonnes and costing about ₹1,760 crore, is expected to be launched in 2028. Now is the time for developing heavy-lift launchers, and for honing skills in docking-undocking, astronauts’ spacewalk, sustainable power transfer and survival in microgravity, alongside carving out a robust research system for offering scientists freedom and on-board database access. This is a challenge Isro must meet to realise the dream of making its space station an ideal successor to the ISS.
